sections.section_title: The Crowd, the Lake, and the Boat
sections.summary: Jesus uses Simon's boat as a teaching platform, drawing Simon into the orbit of his mission before the formal call is issued, as the crowd presses in to hear the word of God.

At Jesus's word, Simon lets down his nets despite a fruitless night of fishing and catches an overwhelming quantity of fish that threatens to break the nets and sink both boats, demonstrating divine authority over creation.

Simon falls at Jesus's feet, confessing himself a sinful man and asking Jesus to depart from him, in a response of awe and self-awareness that echoes the pattern of Isaiah, Manoah, and Ezekiel when encountering divine power.

Jesus tells Simon not to fear and commissions him to catch people alive, and the fishermen leave everything -- nets, boats, the miraculous catch itself -- to follow Jesus, their obedience arising from a revelation of divine power.

Jesus touches a leper and cleanses him, reversing the expected direction of impurity so that cleanness flows from Jesus to the unclean, then instructs the healed man to follow the Mosaic purification procedure as a testimony to the priests.
As the news about Jesus spreads and crowds grow, he habitually withdraws to the wilderness to pray, establishing prayer as the sustaining practice of his ministry.

sections.section_title: The Setting for the Paralytic's Healing
sections.summary: Pharisees and teachers of the law assemble from across the region to observe Jesus, the power of the Lord is present for healing, and men carrying a paralytic demonstrate extraordinary faith by dismantling a roof to lower him before Jesus.

sections.section_title: The Pronouncement of Forgiveness and the Controversy
sections.summary: Jesus responds to the men's faith by declaring the paralytic's sins forgiven, provoking the scribes and Pharisees to charge him with blasphemy on the grounds that only God can forgive sins.

Jesus heals the paralytic as visible evidence that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, establishing a verifiable miracle to authenticate an unverifiable declaration, and the crowd responds with astonishment and fear.

Jesus calls Levi the tax collector from his tax booth with a simple command to follow, and Levi leaves everything behind, extending the social range of Jesus's community to include those classified as collaborators and social outcasts.

Levi hosts a banquet for Jesus with tax collectors and sinners, provoking the Pharisees to object to Jesus's table fellowship, and Jesus responds that he has come not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance -- the physician goes to the sick, not the healthy.

When challenged about his disciples' failure to fast, Jesus introduces the bridegroom metaphor -- celebration is appropriate while the bridegroom is present, but he will be 'taken away,' the first veiled hint of his eventual death.

sections.section_title: The Parables of the Patch and the Wine
sections.summary: Jesus teaches through three short parables that what he is bringing cannot be contained within existing religious structures: new patches ruin both old and new garments, new wine bursts old wineskins, and those accustomed to old wine do not naturally desire new.
